scope: 52 individually checked original core mock-eligible short cards across AQA Physics and Chemistry, prioritising signs, graph meaning, formula directions, optical fibres, ion tests, rates, energetics and taught A2 organic. No Maths Year 2.
method: Guard each reviewed ID and exact original question/answer before appending one equivalent correct wording and two targeted wrong answers; run the production card evaluator on every authored variant. This is a reviewed sample, not all-spec certification.

knownWrongPreviouslyFullyCredited.x: Percentage uncertainty equals measured value divided by absolute uncertainty times 100.
Two equal parallel forces pointing the same way.
Two equal and opposite forces acting along exactly the same line.
For the same momentum change, longer contact time makes mean force larger.
The energy to remove an electron from neutral gaseous atoms to form 1+ ions.
Use the starting partial pressures before the equilibrium is reached.
The aldehyde must always be oxidised all the way to a carboxylic acid during immediate distillation.

limitations: Unseen user answers are not exhaustively certified.
Some existing unreviewed original science cards still lack explicit accept/reject examples.
Never change saved progress keys, original core IDs, existing supplement banks or mock scope.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is true of current in a series circuit?
rows.originalBack: The current is the same at every point.
accept: The current does not split along a series path.
reject: Current splits between the components in series.
Current can be different at each point of one series branch.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What happens to p.d. in a series circuit?
rows.originalBack: The supply p.d. equals the sum of component p.d.s.
accept: The supply voltage equals the sum of the voltage drops across series components.
reject: Potential difference is necessarily identical across every series component.
The component voltage drops must exceed the supply voltage.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is true of p.d. across parallel branches?
rows.originalBack: It is the same across each branch.
accept: The potential difference is identical across all parallel branches.
reject: The supply voltage is divided between separate parallel branches.
Parallel branches must each have a different p.d.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What equation links resistance and resistivity?
rows.originalBack: R = ρL/A.
accept: Resistance is resistivity multiplied by wire length divided by cross-sectional area.
reject: R = ρA/L.
Resistance is proportional to cross-sectional area at constant length.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: How do you calculate percentage uncertainty?
rows.originalBack: percentage uncertainty = absolute uncertainty ÷ measured value × 100%
accept: Percentage uncertainty equals absolute uncertainty divided by the measurement multiplied by 100.
reject: Percentage uncertainty equals measured value divided by absolute uncertainty times 100.
Percentage uncertainty equals absolute uncertainty times the measured value.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: For multiplication or division, how are percentage uncertainties combined?
rows.originalBack: Add the percentage uncertainties.
accept: Add the percentage uncertainties of factors in a product or quotient.
reject: Multiply the percentage uncertainties together.
Add only absolute uncertainties in different units.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What does the area under a velocity–time graph represent?
rows.originalBack: Signed displacement, with area below the time axis counting as negative.
accept: The signed area gives displacement, with area below zero counted negatively.
reject: Area below the axis must be made positive when finding signed displacement.
The area under a velocity–time graph gives acceleration.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What does area under an acceleration–time graph give?
rows.originalBack: Change in velocity, including sign.
accept: Integrating acceleration over time gives signed change in velocity.
reject: The area under an acceleration–time graph is displacement.
The area always gives final velocity without knowing initial velocity.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is needed for a stable two-source interference fringe pattern?
rows.originalBack: Two coherent sources with constant phase difference and same frequency.
accept: The sources need the same frequency and a constant phase difference.
reject: Different frequencies produce a stable interference pattern if their amplitudes match.
A phase difference that changes randomly gives permanent bright and dark fringes.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What path difference produces constructive interference?
rows.originalBack: An integer multiple of λ.
accept: Path difference nλ for integer n.
reject: Path difference of an odd multiple of half a wavelength.
Path difference (n + 0.5)λ causes constructive interference.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What path difference produces destructive interference?
rows.originalBack: An odd multiple of λ/2.
accept: Path difference (n + 1/2)λ where n is an integer.
reject: A whole-number multiple of λ produces destructive interference.
Equal path lengths guarantee destructive interference.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: How does fringe spacing change if double-slit separation increases?
rows.originalBack: It decreases.
accept: The fringe spacing becomes smaller, since w is inversely proportional to slit separation.
reject: Fringe spacing gets larger when the slits move further apart.
Fringe spacing does not change when the separation is doubled.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What happens to ray direction when light enters a more optically dense medium obliquely?
rows.originalBack: It bends towards the normal.
accept: The refracted ray bends closer to the normal.
reject: The ray bends away from the normal in the more optically dense medium.
The refracted ray must always run along the boundary.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What happens to light speed when refractive index increases?
rows.originalBack: It decreases.
accept: Light slows down as the refractive index increases.
reject: Its speed rises as refractive index increases.
Speed of light is the same in all transparent materials.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is material dispersion in an optical fibre?
rows.originalBack: Pulse spreading because different wavelengths travel at different speeds.
accept: Different wavelengths travel at different speeds within the fibre and broaden the pulse.
reject: Material dispersion means different ray paths have different lengths even at one wavelength.
Material dispersion is the absorption of photons by the core.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is modal dispersion in a step-index optical fibre?
rows.originalBack: Pulse spreading because light travels along different paths of different lengths.
accept: Different guided ray paths have different journey times, broadening the pulse.
reject: Modal dispersion occurs because different wavelengths travel at different speeds.
Every ray travels exactly the same path length through a step-index fibre.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What does the line of action of a force mean?
rows.originalBack: An imaginary line in the direction of the force.
accept: The straight line through the force's point of application in the force direction.
reject: The line perpendicular to the force joining its point to the pivot.
The perpendicular shortest distance from the pivot to the force.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: How many forces form a couple?
rows.originalBack: Two equal, opposite, parallel forces.
accept: Two equal, opposite, parallel forces with different lines of action.
reject: Two equal parallel forces pointing the same way.
Two equal and opposite forces acting along exactly the same line.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Can a couple change an object's linear momentum on its own?
rows.originalBack: No: its resultant force is zero.
accept: No, the resultant force is zero so a pure couple cannot change linear momentum.
reject: A couple produces a nonzero total force and accelerates the centre of mass.
A couple always increases the object's translational speed.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Does the moment of a couple depend on pivot position?
rows.originalBack: No.
accept: No, a couple has the same moment about any pivot.
reject: Yes, a couple's moment changes when the pivot is moved.
The moment of a couple is always zero about its midpoint.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Why can a longer collision time reduce the mean impact force?
rows.originalBack: The same momentum change occurs over more time.
accept: The average force is momentum change divided by contact time, so a longer time gives a smaller force.
reject: For the same momentum change, longer contact time makes mean force larger.
The impact force is independent of collision duration for a fixed impulse.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What kind of waves can be polarised?
rows.originalBack: Transverse waves; longitudinal oscillations cannot be plane-polarised in the same way.
accept: Only transverse waves can be plane-polarised in a specified vibration direction.
reject: Longitudinal sound waves can be plane-polarised in the same way.
Every type of wave can be plane-polarised regardless of oscillation direction.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What does negative ΔH mean?
rows.originalBack: Exothermic: heat is released to the surroundings.
accept: A negative ΔH means an exothermic reaction releases heat to its surroundings.
reject: Negative reaction ΔH always means heat is absorbed.
A negative enthalpy change means products have higher enthalpy than reactants.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What does positive ΔH mean?
rows.originalBack: Endothermic: heat is absorbed from the surroundings.
accept: A positive ΔH means the process absorbs heat from the surroundings.
reject: Positive ΔH means an exothermic reaction releases heat.
The products must be lower in enthalpy than the reactants when ΔH is positive.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Where do products lie on an exothermic enthalpy profile?
rows.originalBack: Lower in enthalpy than the reactants.
accept: Products are at a lower enthalpy level than reactants for an exothermic process.
reject: Exothermic products lie higher than reactants on an enthalpy profile.
An exothermic reaction has no enthalpy difference between products and reactants.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Where do products lie on an endothermic enthalpy profile?
rows.originalBack: Higher in enthalpy than the reactants.
accept: The products lie at a higher enthalpy than the starting reactants.
reject: Endothermic products lie below the reactants.
A positive reaction enthalpy means product enthalpy is less than reactant enthalpy.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What conditions must standard enthalpy values use?
rows.originalBack: 100 kPa, a stated temperature and specified standard states.
accept: Standard enthalpies use 100 kPa and stated temperature, usually 298 K, with substances in standard states.
reject: Standard enthalpies always require 101.3 kPa and any physical state.
A standard enthalpy can use 1 kPa with arbitrary states and no stated temperature.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the formation-enthalpy calculation for ΔH°reaction?
rows.originalBack: Sum of product ΔfH° values minus sum of reactant ΔfH° values.
accept: Reaction ΔH° is the sum of product formation enthalpies minus the sum for reactants, using equation coefficients.
reject: Subtract product formation enthalpies from reactant values.
Ignore stoichiometric coefficients when adding formation enthalpies.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why is the ΔfH° of H₂(g) zero?
rows.originalBack: Hydrogen gas is elemental hydrogen in its standard state.
accept: Hydrogen H₂ gas is the element in its standard state, so its standard formation enthalpy is zero.
reject: The hydrogen–hydrogen bond requires zero energy to break.
All gaseous compounds have zero enthalpy of formation.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Write the lattice formation equation for NaCl.
rows.originalBack: Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → NaCl(s).
accept: Na+(g) + Cl-(g) -> NaCl(s)
reject: NaCl(s) -> Na+(g) + Cl-(g)
Na+(aq) + Cl-(aq) -> NaCl(s)

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Write the lattice dissociation equation for NaCl.
rows.originalBack: NaCl(s) → Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g).
accept: NaCl(s) -> Na+(g) + Cl-(g)
reject: Na+(g) + Cl-(g) -> NaCl(s)
NaCl(s) -> Na+(aq) + Cl-(aq)

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Define second ionisation energy.
rows.originalBack: Energy required to remove 1 mole of electrons from 1 mole of gaseous 1+ ions, forming gaseous 2+ ions.
accept: Energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous singly charged positive ions, producing gaseous doubly charged ions.
reject: The energy to remove an electron from neutral gaseous atoms to form 1+ ions.
The energy to remove two electrons at once from gaseous neutral atoms.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What shape is the rate–[A] graph for a zero-order reactant?
rows.originalBack: A horizontal straight line: rate does not depend on [A].
accept: It is a horizontal straight line since rate does not depend on the reactant concentration.
reject: A line through the origin because rate is proportional to concentration.
An upward parabola because rate is proportional to the square of concentration.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What shape is the rate–[A] graph for first order?
rows.originalBack: A straight line through the origin: rate is proportional to [A].
accept: A straight line through the origin because rate is directly proportional to [A].
reject: A horizontal line because the rate is independent of [A].
An upward parabola because rate is proportional to [A] squared.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: On doubling [A], what happens to rate for order 0, 1 and 2?
rows.originalBack: Order 0: unchanged; order 1: ×2; order 2: ×4.
accept: Zero order: unchanged; first order: double; second order: quadruple.
reject: Zero order: double; first order: quadruple; second order: unchanged.
Rate doubles for every order of reaction when concentration doubles.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, what are Kp units if pressure is measured in kPa?
rows.originalBack: kPa⁻².
accept: kPa to the minus second power.
reject: kPa squared.
Kp must have no units for this equation when pressures are in kPa.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Which pressures must be used in a Kp expression?
rows.originalBack: Equilibrium partial pressures.
accept: Use the partial pressure of each gas at equilibrium.
reject: Use the starting partial pressures before the equilibrium is reached.
Use the total pressure in place of each separate partial pressure.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Does a catalyst change the equilibrium constant or position of equilibrium?
rows.originalBack: No. It accelerates forward and reverse reactions, so equilibrium is reached sooner without changing K.
accept: No, a catalyst accelerates forward and reverse rates but does not shift equilibrium or change K.
reject: A catalyst increases K by shifting the balance towards the products.
Catalysts lower activation energy only for the forward reaction and alter the equilibrium position.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Can bromine displace chloride ions from solution?
rows.originalBack: No; bromine is a weaker oxidising agent.
accept: No, bromine is a weaker oxidising agent than chlorine and cannot displace chloride.
reject: Yes, bromine displaces chloride ions because it is more reactive than chlorine.
Yes, bromine is a stronger oxidising agent than chlorine.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Which silver halide dissolves in dilute ammonia?
rows.originalBack: AgCl.
accept: Silver chloride, AgCl, dissolves in dilute ammonia.
reject: AgBr.
AgI.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Which silver halide dissolves in concentrated ammonia, but not dilute?
rows.originalBack: AgBr.
accept: Silver bromide, AgBr, dissolves in concentrated ammonia but not dilute.
reject: Silver iodide, AgI.
Silver chloride, AgCl.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Which silver halide is insoluble in ammonia?
rows.originalBack: AgI.
accept: Silver iodide, AgI, is insoluble in aqueous ammonia.
reject: AgCl.
AgBr.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why is Al first IE lower than Mg first IE?
rows.originalBack: Al loses a higher-energy 3p electron; Mg loses a lower-energy 3s electron.
accept: Al loses a 3p electron, which is higher energy and easier to remove than Mg's 3s electron.
reject: Al has an additional occupied electron shell and hence more shielding than Mg.
Mg loses an outer 3p electron while aluminium loses a 3s electron.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why is S first IE lower than P first IE?
rows.originalBack: Electron repulsion within a paired 3p orbital in S helps one electron escape.
accept: Sulfur has two electrons paired in a 3p orbital, and repulsion makes one easier to remove than from phosphorus.
reject: Sulfur loses a 4s electron while phosphorus loses a 3p electron.
Phosphorus has a doubly occupied 3p orbital that sulfur does not have.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What reagent reduces aldehydes and ketones?
rows.originalBack: NaBH₄, sodium tetrahydridoborate.
accept: Sodium borohydride, NaBH4.
reject: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI).
Hydrogen cyanide and KCN.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What mechanism occurs when HCN adds to a carbonyl compound?
rows.originalBack: Nucleophilic addition.
accept: Nucleophilic addition to the C=O carbonyl bond.
reject: Electrophilic substitution of the carbonyl oxygen.
Free radical substitution.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What organic class comes from aldehyde reduction?
rows.originalBack: A primary alcohol.
accept: A primary alcohol forms when an aldehyde is reduced.
reject: A secondary alcohol.
A ketone.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What organic class comes from ketone reduction?
rows.originalBack: A secondary alcohol.
accept: The reduction of a ketone forms a secondary alcohol.
reject: A primary alcohol.
A carboxylic acid.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What forms when a primary alcohol is oxidised gently and distilled?
rows.originalBack: An aldehyde.
accept: An aldehyde is collected by distillation after controlled oxidation of a primary alcohol.
reject: A ketone.
The aldehyde must always be oxidised all the way to a carboxylic acid during immediate distillation.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What forms when a primary alcohol is oxidised under reflux with excess oxidant?
rows.originalBack: A carboxylic acid.
accept: An excess oxidant under reflux converts a primary alcohol into a carboxylic acid.
reject: An aldehyde is necessarily the final product under excess oxidant and reflux.
A ketone.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What forms when a secondary alcohol is oxidised?
rows.originalBack: A ketone.
accept: A ketone forms when a secondary alcohol is oxidised.
reject: An aldehyde.
A carboxylic acid.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Rank lone–lone, lone–bond and bond–bond pair repulsion.
rows.originalBack: Lone–lone > lone–bond > bond–bond.
accept: Lone pair–lone pair repulsion is strongest, then lone–bond, then bond–bond.
reject: Bond–bond > lone–bond > lone–lone.
All electron-pair repulsions are equally strong.
